848.title: The beginning of knowledge (Proverbs 1:7)
848.hook: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge"
848.carry: the first step through the door
848.howItsDone: Mishlei is part of the Writings. Jews study it as practical wisdom for daily life, and its sayings are quoted at tables, in classrooms and in synagogue teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the book of Job ended with a surprise: the friends with tidy answers were wrong, and the man who cried out was right. Today, a new book, and a very different voice.

A grandmother's saying. A line taped above a desk. Something a coach shouted once that a player still repeats years later. Short sayings travel. They fit in a pocket, and they come out at the right moment, often when the long explanation has been forgotten. After Job, with its long speeches and its storm, the Writings turn to a whole book of these pocket sentences, one or two lines each. Easy to say, hard to live. Today's word is that book's Hebrew name.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER'S SAYING.` → `SHORT SAYINGS TRAVEL.` → `A WHOLE BOOK OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Mishlei. It's the Hebrew name of the book English calls Proverbs, taken from its opening words: the proverbs of Solomon the son of David, king of Israel. Tradition links it to Solomon, the king remembered for asking God for wisdom. The book also names other voices further on, so it reads less like one lecture and more like a family's collected advice. The opening verses say why it exists: to know wisdom, to understand words of insight, so the simple can grow shrewd and the young gain knowledge. Then, before any advice, the line the whole book stands on: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge." Fear here is worth sitting with. Some readers hear awe, the feeling of standing before something far bigger than yourself. Others hear a plainer fear: the care not to do wrong in God's sight, a respect that changes how a person acts. Jewish teachers have read it more than one way. And notice the word beginning. Not the end of knowledge, as if faith replaces thinking. Awe is where learning starts, the first step through the door, not a wall at the end of the hall. Job ended with God showing him stars and sea, and Job going quiet. Mishlei starts from that quiet and builds a daily life on it: how to speak, how to work, how to treat a neighbor. Proverbs are small, but they assume something large behind them.

Keep it turning until you can say it without reaching for it. If you pray, you can let it be a prayer; if not, let it simply be yours.

Your line: the first step through the door. Awe first, then knowledge. Day eight hundred forty-eight.

849.title: A tree of life (Proverbs 3:17–18)
849.hook: sung as the Torah returns to the ark: "Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace"
849.howItsDone: In synagogue services, as the Torah scroll is returned to the ark, congregations sing Etz chayim hi, the verses from Proverbs 3:18 and 3:17, before the ark is closed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mishlei opened with the fear of the LORD as the beginning of knowledge. Your line was the first step through the door. Today, two verses from the same book that left the page and became a song.

The reading is over. The scroll has been lifted, rolled and dressed again in its cover. It's carried back toward the ark at the front of the synagogue, and the doors stand open. As it goes in, the congregation sings. The song's opening lines aren't new words written for the moment. They're two verses lifted straight out of the book of Proverbs. Wisdom and Torah, sung in one breath, and then the doors close on the scroll.
screen: `THE READING IS OVER.` → `THE SCROLL RETURNS TO THE ARK.` → `TWO VERSES FROM PROVERBS.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in the King James words: "She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her." And just before it: "Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace." In Proverbs, the she is wisdom, described like a person: more precious than rubies, long life in one hand, riches and honor in the other. Then the synagogue does something quiet and bold: it sings those verses about the Torah. The Torah becomes the tree, and the people singing are the ones holding on. Notice the verb: lay hold upon her. A tree of life isn't admired from a distance. You grab it. The tradition gives this a physical shape too: the wooden rollers a Torah scroll is wound on are called atzei chayim, trees of life. Every time someone lifts the scroll, their hands are literally on the trees. And her ways are ways of pleasantness became a test for some Jewish teachers: in the Talmud, a reading of the law that would bring needless hardship is set aside, because her ways are pleasant. All her paths are peace. Peace here is shalom, a word with room in it for wholeness, for things being as they should be. So the song asks a lot of the people who sing it: hold on to the tree, and choose the path that leads to peace.

segments.voice: Let one choice from today come to mind, a message to answer, a chore, a conversation, a line at the store, and picture two ways through it, one sharper, one gentler, without deciding yet. Then let your hands close lightly, as if holding on to something steady. If you pray, you can say the line silently, all her paths are peace; if not, just breathe and hold the picture.

850.title: A soft answer (Proverbs 15:1)
850.carry: a soft tongue breaketh the bone
850.howItsDone: Jewish teaching on careful speech draws on verses like Proverbs 15:1, and the line is quoted at home and in the classroom when an argument starts to rise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two verses from Proverbs became the song sung as the Torah returns to the ark. Your line was all her paths are peace. Today, Proverbs shows what that path sounds like.

The text arrives at 9:40 at night. It's short, and it's sharp, and it ends with a period that somehow feels like a slammed door. A reply starts forming almost at once: accurate, cutting, impossible to argue with. Sending it would be satisfying for a minute or two. Then the phone buzzes again, and it's worse, and now two people are awake and angry. Proverbs has a sentence for the moment before you hit send.
screen: `A SHARP TEXT AT NIGHT.` → `THE PERFECT REPLY.` → `THE MOMENT BEFORE SEND.`

segments.voice: Proverbs fifteen, verse one, in the King James words: "A soft answer turneth away wrath." The second half finishes the thought: grievous words stir up anger. Two roads side by side, and you can see where each one ends. The Hebrew for soft here is rakh: tender, gentle. It doesn't mean silent, and it doesn't mean giving in. A soft answer still says something; it just says it in a way that lets the other person lower their guard. Later the book pushes further, with a picture that sounds almost impossible: a soft tongue breaketh the bone. Gentleness can do what force can't. The Tanakh has a story that shows it. In the book of Judges, after a battle, the men of Ephraim come to Gideon furious: why didn't you call us to fight? They chide him sharply. Gideon could have fired back. Instead he answers by praising them: what have I done, compared with you? And the text says their anger toward him abated. A quarrel ends in one sentence. Notice what Proverbs doesn't say. It doesn't promise a soft answer always works, or that anger is never deserved. It sets the two roads side by side and lets you see where each usually ends. Harsh words feed a fire. Soft ones give it nothing to burn.
screen: `TWO HALVES, TWO ROADS.` · then, large: `A SOFT ANSWER TURNETH AWAY WRATH.` · `RAKH: TENDER, NOT SILENT.` · then: `GIDEON AND THE MEN OF EPHRAIM.`

851.title: His own way (Proverbs 22:6)
851.hook: train a child "in the way he should go"; commentators read it as each child's own way
851.howItsDone: Jewish teachers and parents quote Proverbs 22:6, reading 'according to his way' as a reason to teach each child in a way that fits that child.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a soft answer turneth away wrath, and Gideon cooled a quarrel with one sentence. Your line was a soft tongue breaketh the bone. Today, a verse about raising children, and a small Hebrew word that changes it.

Two kids, same house, same parents, same bedtime story read the same way. One wants to hear it again and again. The other has already wandered off to take the radio apart. The same lesson can land on one and slide right off the other. Proverbs has a famous verse about training children. Read quickly, it sounds like a rule for everyone. Read slowly, in Hebrew, it might be saying something else.
screen: `TWO KIDS, ONE HOUSE.` → `ONE LESSON, TWO RESULTS.` → `READ IT SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it." It sounds simple: pick the right path, put the child on it, and hold them there until it sticks. But the phrase translated in the way he should go is, word for word, closer to according to his way. Al pi darko. His way. Whose way is that? Some commentators read it as the way a child ought to go, the path set out for everyone. Others notice that little his and read it as the child's own way: his nature, his pace, the shape of his mind. Teach each child according to who that child is. The one who wants the story again and the one taking the radio apart may both learn, but not by the same road. Another layer: the verb for train is chanokh, and elsewhere the Tanakh uses it for dedicating a new house. So training a child, on this reading, is less like pushing and more like a beginning, opening something and setting it on its way. Then the promise: when he is old, he will not depart from it. On the second reading, the promise has a reason inside it: a way that was the child's own from the start is a way the child can keep. The verse doesn't settle which reading is right, and Jewish teachers have held both.
screen: `TRAIN UP A CHILD.` · then, large: `AL PI DARKO: ACCORDING TO HIS WAY.` · `CHANOKH: TO TRAIN, TO DEDICATE.` · then: `HE WILL NOT DEPART FROM IT.`

852.title: Give him bread (Proverbs 25:21)
852.hook: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat"
852.carry: the need comes first, and the history comes second
852.howItsDone: Jewish teaching links Proverbs 25:21 with the Torah's commands to help an enemy's stray or overloaded animal (Exodus 23:4–5), and the line is studied as part of how to treat people you're in conflict with.

segments.voice: Yesterday, train up a child according to his way. Your line was each child's own way. Today, Proverbs sets a place for a guest nobody invites.

Someone knocks just as the bread comes out of the oven. Handing a slice to a friend would take no thought at all. Now change one thing. The person standing at the door, hungry, is someone you'd rather not see: the neighbor who complained about you, the coworker who took the credit, someone who once wished you harm and said so. Does the bread still get handed over? Proverbs answers in one plain sentence.
screen: `BREAD FRESH FROM THE OVEN.` → `CHANGE ONE THING.` → `WHO IS AT THE DOOR?`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink." No other conditions. Not if he apologizes, not if he's earned it. If he's hungry. The need comes first, and the history comes second. The verse goes on with a strange picture: for thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee. Readers differ on the coals. Some hear the burning shame of being treated kindly by someone you wronged, a shame that might turn into regret. Others hear warmth, a kindness that melts the hostility. The picture stays open. The Torah already says something close. In Exodus, if you find your enemy's ox or donkey wandering, you bring it back, and if the donkey of someone who hates you is lying under its load, you help lift it. The rule doesn't ask you to like the person, only to help with the animal. In Kings, an army from Aram comes after the prophet Elisha and is struck so it can't see where it's going. Elisha leads the soldiers into Samaria, into the hands of the king of Israel, who asks, shall I strike them? No, says Elisha: set bread and water before them, and send them home. The king prepares a great meal, and they eat, drink and go home to their master. And the raiding bands of Aram came no more into the land of Israel. The very next verse brings a full war, so the peace isn't forever. But the raids ended at a table, not at sword point.

853.title: All is breath (Ecclesiastes 1:2)
853.hook: "vanity of vanities"; the Hebrew hevel means breath or vapor
853.howItsDone: Kohelet (Ecclesiastes) is one of the five scrolls of the Writings, and Ashkenazi communities read it in synagogue during the festival of Sukkot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, if thine enemy be hungry, give him bread, and Elisha fed an army and sent it home. Your line was the need comes first, and the history comes second. Today, a stranger, more searching book.
screen: `THE NEED COMES FIRST, AND THE HISTORY COMES SECOND.`

segments.voice: Breathe on a cold window. A small gray cloud appears on the glass, and for a moment you could write your name in it. Then, while you watch, it shrinks from the edges and is gone. The glass looks exactly as it did before. One book of the Tanakh takes that little cloud and holds it up to everything: work, money, wisdom, pleasure, fame, a whole lifetime. Its opening cry is one word, said again and again. Today's word.
screen: `BREATH ON A COLD WINDOW.` → `GONE WHILE YOU WATCH.` → `ONE WORD, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Hevel. The book is Ecclesiastes, in Hebrew Kohelet, named for its speaker, the one the King James calls the Preacher. Here's how he begins: "Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity." Every vanity in that line is the same Hebrew word, hevel. And hevel isn't about pride or mirrors. Its plain picture is breath. Vapor. The mist that rises off a cup and isn't there a moment later. So the line can be heard another way: breath of breaths, all is breath. That changes the feeling of the book. Vanity sounds like a verdict: worthless. Breath is real. You can feel it on your hand; it keeps you alive. It just can't be held. Kohelet looks at everything people chase and says, again and again, hevel. You build, and someone else inherits. You grow wise, and the wise die like the foolish. You gather, and it slips away. There's an echo here, too. In Genesis, the brother who is killed, whom English calls Abel, is in Hebrew named Hevel. A life like a breath. Some readers find Kohelet bleak. Others find him honest, even freeing: if everything is breath, you can stop gripping. Either way, the word asks for a light touch. Not that nothing is real, but that nothing stays in the hand.
screen: `KOHELET, THE PREACHER.` · then, large: `VANITY OF VANITIES: BREATH OF BREATHS.` · `REAL, BUT IMPOSSIBLE TO HOLD.` · then: `ABEL, IN HEBREW, IS HEVEL.`

segments.voice: Breathe in through your nose, no strain, then let the breath out slowly through your mouth, longer than the breath in, and feel that you can't hold on to it and don't need to: another comes. If a worry rises, let it ride out on the breath. If you pray, you can let one breath out carry a word of prayer.
Hevel. Breath, vapor, mist: the word the King James text renders as vanity, Kohelet's word for everything people try to hold. Today's word.

854.title: A season (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8)
854.hook: "To every thing there is a season"
854.howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 3 belongs to Kohelet, one of the five scrolls of the Writings, and some Jews quote its 'a time to' lines at turning points in life, from celebrations to houses of mourning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kohelet's opening cry: hevel, breath of breaths. Your line was nothing stays in the hand. Today, the same book turns its breath into a rhythm, and the week comes to a close.

Same afternoon, same street. On one porch, a family is setting out chairs for a party, balloons tied to the railing. Three doors down, the curtains are drawn, and cars line the curb at a house of mourning. A man walks past both houses on the way to buy milk. Nobody on that street is doing life wrong. They're just in different hours of it. Kohelet has a poem for that street. It reads like a list, and it works like a clock.
screen: `A PARTY ON ONE PORCH.` → `MOURNING THREE DOORS DOWN.` → `DIFFERENT HOURS OF ONE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Ecclesiastes chapter three, in the King James words: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: A time to be born, and a time to die." A time to plant, and a time to pluck up. A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance. A time to keep silence, and a time to speak. And at the end: a time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace. Every line holds two opposites side by side, and neither cancels the other. The poem doesn't say mourning is bad and dancing is good. Each has its hour. Yesterday, Kohelet called everything breath. Today he hints at something steadier underneath: a little further on, he says God hath made every thing beautiful in his time. Not every moment is beautiful on its own, but each one has a place. Readers take the poem two ways. Some find comfort: grief won't last forever, and neither will this hard stretch. Others hear a challenge: you don't choose the season, but you can ask what this one is for. A time to speak, or to keep silence? To plant, or to wait? The poem doesn't answer for you. It just insists the question is real.
screen: `TO EVERY THING THERE IS A SEASON.` · `PAIRS OF OPPOSITES, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `EVERY THING BEAUTIFUL IN HIS TIME.` · then: `WHAT IS THIS SEASON FOR?`

segments.voice: This week ran from Mishlei and the first step through the door, through atzei chayim, rakh, each child's own way and bread for an enemy, to breath that can't be held. Now let a pair from the poem find you, plant or pluck up, weep or laugh, keep silence or speak, and notice not the one you wish for but the one that's true. Say quietly, this is a time to, and finish the line; if you pray, you can bring that season with you into prayer.
